sentences.text: Idiacanthus is a genus of barbeled dragonfishes whose larvae exhibit the Stylophthalmine trait, a name derived from Greek words meaning 'own' and 'spine' or 'thorn'.
Three recognized species exist within this group: Idiacanthus antrostomus, Idiacanthus atlanticus, and Idiacanthus fasciola.
Taxonomically, the genus belongs to the family Stomiidae, subfamily Idiacanthinae, order Stomiiformes, and class Actinopterygii.
While some sources describe the maximum length of these fish as between 38 and 53 cm, other measurements indicate females reach 40 cm and males only 5 cm.
Females possess black skin, whereas males are dark brown.
Males lack teeth, a chin barbel, and a functioning gut.

Both sexes feature small photophores spread throughout their bodies and a strip of chevron-shaped luminescent tissue along the dorsal and ventral sides that glows yellow or blue-green when stimulated.
A fertile female Idiacanthus fasciola can hold approximately 14,000 eggs.
These fish have pectoral fins in their larval stage but lose them in adulthood.
The premaxilla, maxilla, and mandible teeth of the family are almost all capable of being depressed.
Known as devil fish or black dragons, these marine fish of the stomiid family live in the mesopelagic and bathypelagic zones of the abyssal waters of all oceans.
Idiacanthus fasciola is widely distributed in the North and South Atlantic, the Indo-Pacific, and other areas, while Idiacanthus antrostomus is mainly found in the Eastern Pacific.

A fossil genus named Idiacanthus by Gunnell in 1933 is classified under Chondrichthyes and lived from the Moscovian to Kasimovian (312.8 to 306 million years ago), raising questions about the name's application to modern fish.
